summary.case_overview: Writ Petition (Civil) No. 135 of 1970 (*Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru and Ors. v. State of Kerala and Anr.*) was decided by a 13-judge Bench of the Supreme Court of India on April 24, 1973 [Page 1]. The petition initially challenged the constitutionality of Kerala land reform legislation under fundamental rights provisions including Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 25, 26, and 31 [Page 1]. summary.facts_of_case: On March 21, 1970, the petitioner filed Writ Petition No. 135 of 1970 under Article 32 of the Constitution for enforcement of fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 25, 26, and 31, praying that the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 (Act 1 of 1964) as amended by the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969 (Act 35 of 1969) be declared unconstitutional and void [Page 1]. Rule nisi was issued on March 25, 1970 [Page 1]. During the pendency of the petition, the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1971 (Kerala Act 25 of 1971) was passed and received Presidential assent on August 7, 1971 [Page 1]. Subsequently, Parliament enacted the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act (effective November 5, 1971), the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act (effective April 20, 1972), and the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act (effective June 9, 1972) [Page 1] [Page 2]. The Twenty-ninth Amendment inserted Kerala Acts 35 of 1969 and 25 of 1971 into the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution as entries 65 and 66 [Page 2]. The Supreme Court granted permission to amend the writ petition to challenge these Constitutional Amendments [Page 2]. The Constitution Bench referred the matter to a larger bench of 13 judges to determine the validity of the impugned constitutional amendments and to re-examine whether *I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab* was correctly decided [Page 2].
summary.legal_issues: What is the true scope and extent of the amending power conferred on Parliament by Article 368 of the Constitution [Page 2]? Was *I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab* correctly decided in holding that Parliament had no power to amend Part III so as to take away or abridge fundamental rights by virtue of Article 13(2) [Page 2] [Page 6] [Page 7]? summary.important_arguments_or_content: The petitioners contended that the power of Parliament under Article 368 is limited and cannot be exercised to alter or destroy the basic structure, essential features, or identity of the Constitution [Page 2] [Page 5] [Page 91] [Page 258] [Page 487]. They argued that fundamental rights were intended to subsist forever to protect citizens from government tyranny [Page 2]. They submitted that Article 31C subverted core freedoms, delegated amending power to state legislatures, and eliminated judicial review through a conclusive declaration clause [Page 2] [Page 245] [Page 496]. They further maintained that fundamental rights are natural or inalienable rights superior to ordinary legislative and amending powers [Page 181] [Page 487]. The respondents contended that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 is wide, plenary, unlimited, and an adjunct of sovereignty, containing no implied or inherent limitations [Page 2] [Page 7] [Page 91] [Page 104] [Page 488]. They argued that Parliament can alter or abrogate any provision, including fundamental rights, replace democracy, or alter the form of government if deemed necessary for socio-economic progress and achieving Directive Principles [Page 2] [Page 4] [Page 104] [Page 271] [Page 497]. They submitted that the term 'amendment' in Article 368 includes addition, variation, or repeal of any provision without restriction [Page 78] [Page 129] [Page 484].

The judges concluded that Article 368 (both as originally enacted and as amended) contains both the power and procedure for constitutional amendment, deriving power from Article 368 itself and not from residuary legislative powers (Entry 97 List I / Article 248) [Page 129] [Page 309] [Page 486] [Page 501]. summary.simplified_explanation: A religious leader in Kerala challenged state land reform laws that restricted his monastery's property rights [Page 1]. While his case was pending in the Supreme Court, Parliament passed three constitutional amendments (the 24th, 25th, and 29th Amendments) to protect land reform laws from court challenges and confirm Parliament's authority to amend any part of the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 2]. The Supreme Court formed a special 13-judge Bench to decide whether Parliament has unlimited power to change the Constitution [Page 2]. The Court overruled its previous decision in *Golak Nath*, deciding that Parliament does have the power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, because amending the Constitution is a special 'constituent power' distinct from making ordinary laws [Page 129] [Page 374] [Page 501]. However, a majority of the judges held that Parliament's power to amend is not unlimited: Parliament cannot alter, destroy, or emasculate the 'basic structure' or essential features of the Constitution [Page 104] [Page 129] [Page 258] [Page 374]. The Court upheld the 24th, 25th, and 29th Amendments, but ruled that courts retain the right to review laws passed under Article 31C to ensure they actually serve Directive Principles and do not destroy the basic structure of the Constitution [Page 258] [Page 374] [Page 498] [Page 501] [Page 502].
